sources.news_title: A TV news helicopter covering one LA tragedy became a second one Tuesday night
sources.text:
A television news helicopter covering a deadly Los Angeles-area crash went down in flames of its own Tuesday evening, killing the two crew members aboard and a third person on the ground, according to NBC Los Angeles. The aircraft, known on air as NewsChopper4 and flown for NBC4 and its Spanish-language sister station Telemundo 52, crashed shortly before 7 p.m. in Chatsworth, just blocks from the scene it had been streaming live minutes earlier.
Two crashes, one night, one stretch of the Valley
The chain of events began around 5 p.m., when an SUV slammed into the side of a Los Angeles Metro bus near Nordhoff Street and De Soto Avenue, according to Fox 11 Los Angeles. NewsChopper4 launched to cover the collision, as local stations routinely do for major traffic incidents. Less than two hours later, at 6:57 p.m., the aircraft dropped into the narrow gap separating two commercial buildings on the 9100 block of Mason Avenue; the resulting blaze consumed four parked cars and a pair of cargo containers nearby, Fox 11 reported. More than 70 firefighters responded, according to The Associated Press.
Who were Eliana Moreno and George Marciniw
Moreno grew up in Orange County and earned her college degree in 2010, pairing broadcast journalism coursework with political science at Chapman University before going straight into the cockpit as an aerial reporter for Angel City Air, the firm that supplies the helicopter and crew for NBC4 and Telemundo 52, according to NBC News. She had partnered with pilot George Marciniw since 2023 and was known on social media as "Eli in the heli." Marciniw brought more than three decades of flight experience to the cockpit. NBC4 anchor Colleen Williams called Moreno a "valued friend and colleague" during a live broadcast after her death was confirmed. The identity of the third victim, who was on the ground when the aircraft came down, had not been released as of Wednesday.
What caused the bus collision remains unclear
Los Angeles Fire Department officials put the bus crash's on-scene toll at two, with six more people hospitalized. A Metro spokesperson later told MyNewsLA that the SUV's driver had since succumbed to injuries in a hospital, a development that would push that crash's toll to three and the night's combined count to six — a figure not yet reflected in every account. Investigators have not said what caused the SUV to strike the bus.
City leaders react as federal investigators take over
Mayor Karen Bass addressed the dual tragedy hours later, saying, "We lost five Angelenos today," and adding that Chatsworth would feel the loss for some time to come, per CBS Los Angeles. She also posted a longer statement of condolence on X to the families of everyone lost in both the bus collision and the helicopter crash.
Governor Gavin Newsom likewise extended condolences "with the entire NBC4 family" and thanked first responders in a post on X.
A witness identified as Allyona Sevanesian described watching the aircraft falter before it went down, telling Fox 11 that "the helicopter was swaying" moments before impact. Breaking-news aggregator BNO News was among the first accounts to publish a casualty count as the story developed Tuesday night.
The National Transportation Safety Board and Federal Aviation Administration confirmed they would jointly investigate the helicopter crash beginning Wednesday, a process that in comparable cases has taken months to produce even preliminary findings. Neither the Los Angeles Police Department nor Metro has publicly determined what caused the original SUV-bus collision that NewsChopper4 was covering when it went down.

sources.news_title: News Helicopter Crashes While Covering Fatal Bus Crash, Killing 3 People
sources.text:
News Helicopter Crashes While Covering Fatal Bus Crash, Killing 3 People
An SUV slammed into the side of an LA Metro bus on Tuesday, killing at least two people and injuring six. The tragedy was compounded when a news helicopter crashed near the scene of the collision, killing pilot George Marciniw and reporter Eliana Moreno on board, as well as a person on the ground. KNBC confirmed that the crashed helicopter was the station's NewsChopper4. The live footage of the rotorcraft going down is harrowing, but it's unclear why it crashed.
NewsChopper4 was owned and operated by Angel City Air, a "self-described full-service aerial production company," providing aerial news coverage for NBC4 and Telemundo 52. The helicopter's feed was being broadcast when it crashed. During an aerial shot of the bus crash, you can hear the engine failure alarm go off. Marciniw blurted out, "F*ck!" as the engine spooled down, and Moreno replied, "What, you can't pull up?" The helicopter essentially fell out of the sky, with the feed cutting out before impact.
News anchors often cover tragedies, but not often involving their colleagues
Los Angeles Fire Department said that the news helicopter came down between two commercial buildings, erupting into a fireball. The resulting blaze damaged four cars and two storage containers. Authorities haven't revealed the identity of the person killed on the ground or the two others who were hospitalized. As an onlooker, this incident was emotionally devastating. I can't imagine what it was like in the newsroom. According to the Beast Daily, NBC4 anchor Colleen Williams said on air, "We knew it was a news chopper. We knew we'd lost contact with our people out there, and we've just received confirmation."
Helicopters always make me uneasy. While planes can glide when they lose engine power, rotorcraft pilots can only pray that the blades auto-rotate. Otherwise, there's no hope. A Bell 206L4 sightseeing helicopter crashed in the Hudson River last year, killing a Spanish rail executive, his wife and their three children. Investigators later concluded that multiple bird strikes caused the crash. You could have a perfectly functional helicopter and everything could still go wrong.

sources.news_title: Why did a news helicopter crash while covering an LA bus wreck?
sources.text:
A Los Angeles news helicopter crashed near the scene of a deadly bus collision. The incident ended up killing three people and injuring another as emergency crews were still working nearby. The helicopter went down in Chatsworth and burst into flames, adding another fatal crash to an already active emergency scene.
The aircraft was covering the nearby collision when it crashed between two commercial buildings. Per NBC, the helicopter was operated for NBC4 and Telemundo 52, and the station confirmed during its coverage that its NewsChopper4 had gone down.
Los Angeles firefighters said three people were killed in the helicopter crash, while another person was taken to a hospital. The crash also damaged four vehicles and two storage containers, with firefighters responding to a fire that had engulfed the aircraft.
The helicopter was covering another deadly crash
The first emergency involved an SUV that collided with a Metro bus in Chatsworth. Two people were killed and six others were hospitalized in that collision, according to the Los Angeles Fire Department.
The helicopter went down less than a mile from the bus crash site. Firefighters found the aircraft near the 9100 block of Mason Avenue, between two commercial buildings, with flames spreading to nearby property.
NBC4 anchor Colleen Williams confirmed the station’s helicopter had crashed during a live broadcast. “We are going to take a couple of minutes to think about that, process it,” Williams told viewers as the station responded to the news.
The circumstances surrounding the deaths were not immediately clear. Fire department spokesperson Branden Silverman said one person killed in the crash appeared to have been outside the helicopter when it came down.
“We do have one confirmed patient that seemed to be outside of the helicopter when it crashed,” Silverman said. That person was pronounced dead at the scene, while officials had not immediately determined where the other two victims had been.
Officials also had not established how many people were aboard the helicopter when it crashed. NBC4 later confirmed the aircraft belonged to the station, but the victims’ identities were being withheld while authorities worked to notify their next of kin.
The helicopter crash triggered a large response from Los Angeles firefighters. Crews extinguished the flames after the aircraft came down near the commercial buildings, with the fire department reporting damage to vehicles and storage containers in the area.
The National Transportation Safety Board and Federal Aviation Administration are investigating the crash. They are expected to lead the investigation and shed some light into what caused the aircraft to go down.

Los Angeles, California — Three people were killed Tuesday evening when a news helicopter used by NBC4 Los Angeles and Telemundo 52 crashed in the Chatsworth neighborhood while covering a separate deadly collision involving an SUV and a Metro bus.
NBC4 identified the two people aboard the helicopter as aerial journalist Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw, both employees of Angel City Air. A third person was killed on the ground. The Los Angeles Fire Department said the helicopter went down shortly before 7 p.m. near Mason Avenue, igniting a fire that damaged four vehicles and two storage containers.
The crash happened while several news helicopters were covering an earlier collision between an SUV and a city bus in the same area. That crash killed at least two people and sent six others to hospitals, according to the fire department.
Video from the helicopter’s final live transmission captured an alarm sounding as the aircraft rapidly lost altitude. Aviation experts cautioned that the footage alone cannot establish the cause. The National Transportation Safety Board and Federal Aviation Administration are investigating.
Moreno had worked in aerial news coverage since 2010 and regularly reported for both NBC4 and Telemundo 52. Marciniw was a longtime Southern California pilot who had flown with Moreno since 2023.
NBC4 anchors announced the deaths during an emotional live broadcast Tuesday night as colleagues continued reporting from both crash scenes.

sources.news_title: Third victim in LA helicopter crash identified. What we know
sources.text:
Third victim in LA helicopter crash identified. What we know
(This story was updated to add new information.)
Three people who died in the news helicopter crash in Los Angeles have been identified as journalist Eliana Moreno, pilot George Marciniw and a 29-year-old man, according to NBC4 Los Angeles and county officials.
The tragedy unfolded when a helicopter, operated by Angel City Air and covering news for NBC4 and Telemundo 52, crashed before 7 p.m. on Tuesday, Sept. 15, according to the Los Angeles City Fire Department and NBC4.
One person on the ground was killed in the crash in Chatsworth, a community in the San Fernando Valley.
“We are deeply saddened to share that a helicopter providing aerial news coverage for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 was involved in a fatal accident in Los Angeles on Tuesday evening,” NBC4 and Telemundo 52 said in a joint statement. “We extend our heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives.”
What happened in the LA helicopter crash?
A Los Angeles Metro bus and vehicle crashed shortly after 5 p.m. in Chatsworth, killing two people and leaving others in critical condition, Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said at a late-night news conference Tuesday. The helicopter crashed near the vehicle collision scene, Bass said. Los Angeles Fire Department extinguished a fire caused by the crash.
Details about the helicopter emerged during NBC4’s broadcast on Tuesday.
"We've been telling you that we've been piecing it together here. We knew it was a news chopper, we knew we'd lost contact with our people out there, and we just received the confirmation that, in fact, NewsChopper4 went down just before 7 o'clock tonight in Chatsworth," Anchor Colleen Williams said.
The National Transportation Safety Board will lead the investigation, according to authorities.
“Tonight is a tragedy compounded by another tragedy,” LA City Councilmember Bob Blumenfield said.
LA helicopter crash: Third victim identified
Edy Gutierrez Mejia, 29, has been identified as a victim in the helicopter crash, according to the County of Los Angeles Department of Medical Examiner. No city of residence is currently listed for Mejia, whose place of death was identified as a “business parking lot.”
Who are Eliana Moreno and George Marciniw?
Moreno was a Southern California native and alum of Chapman University in Orange County, according to the National Association of Hispanic Journalists — which Moreno was a member of.
NAHJ said she was engaged to be married. Moreno’s social media posts show her vast coverage, including of the massive cold storage warehouse fire in Boyle Heights in June, the Sandy Fire in Simi Valley in May, and the Dodgers victory parade following their World Series win in 2025.
“She was dedicated to her craft, and so passionate about this job,” said Rick Montanez, a CBS LA reporter who had known Moreno and spoke about her in a broadcast on Wednesday, Sept. 16.
Moreno joined the Angel City Air team in 2010, according to her LinkedIn page.
She and Marciniw — who is “believed to have had more than 30 years of flight experience”— began flying together in 2023, according to NBC4.
Marciniw grew up in Southern California and graduated from Burbank High School, NBC4 reported.
USA TODAY reporter Jeanine Santucci contributed to this story.
Paris Barraza is a reporter covering Los Angeles and Southern California for the USA TODAY Network. Reach her at pbarraza@usatodayco.com.

sources.text: By — Ashley Duong, Associated Press Ashley Duong, Associated Press By — Hallie Golden, Associated Press Hallie Golden, Associated Press Leave your feedback Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/3-people-killed-in-news-helicopter-crash-while-covering-la-bus-collision Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Driver arrested in a bus collision that happened before a deadly news helicopter crash in LA Nation Sep 16, 2026 12:54 PM EDT LOS ANGELES (AP) — A motorist was arrested on murder charges after authorities say she slammed her SUV into a city bus in Los Angeles, killing at least two people and injuring six others in a prelude to a second deadly tragedy: the fiery crash of a TV news helicopter that was covering the collision. Bailee Lynn Rios, 36, of Simi Valley, was arrested Tuesday night and is being held at a Los Angeles jail with bail set at $4 million, police said Wednesday. The case is being forwarded to the district attorney's office, which will decide whether to file the charges in court or pursue different ones. Information on a lawyer who could speak on her behalf was not immediately available. The helicopter, which was used by NBC and Telemundo, crashed about two hours after police say Rios drove her 2004 Ford Expedition the wrong way down a busy avenue, ran a red light and struck a vehicle before hitting the bus. One passenger was fully ejected from the bus and another was partially ejected, police said. READ MORE: All 5 killed in Miami airport cargo jet crash were in a van used by plane cleaners Rios' mother, Cindy Rios, said she was shocked and saddened by the string of events. She said she had not spoken to Bailee Lynn since her arrest and had not been contacted by law enforcement. "It's just horrible," Cindy Rios told The Associated Press in a phone interview Wednesday. "The fact that my daughter was involved and was the cause of it is just extremely disturbing." "If anything, I'm sorry for the other families," she added. "My daughter's alive. People lost their lives." Chopper crash killed a reporter, a pilot and a man on the ground NBC4 Los Angeles reported that two people aboard the helicopter — reporter Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw — were killed when the chopper went down Tuesday in the Chatsworth neighborhood in the San Fernando Valley north of downtown. A person on the ground, identified as 29-year-old Edy Gutierrez Mejia, died in a parking lot, the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner's Office said. He was from Guatemala, the country's consulate confirmed. The crash happened as news crews were reporting on the collision involving the SUV that slammed into the bus. READ MORE: Pilots of helicopter that crashed while fighting wildfire in Utah are dead, officials say There were no immediate details on what caused the helicopter crash, but an alarm could be heard sounding inside the helicopter's cockpit as it lost altitude in the final seconds of video the crew broadcast before the crash. Just after the beeping noise starts, a woman's voice says "uh oh." The helicopter moves quickly away from the bus crash site and starts losing altitude. The woman says "You can't pull up?" before the video stops as the chopper nears the ground. "That video is probably the most important evidence that we have discovered so far," National Transportation Safety Board investigator Fabian Salazar said Wednesday at a news briefing. Salazar said the sounds were consistent with the helicopter's engine changing speed, as well as what he said were likely advisory tones for the pilot. The NTSB said it is also investigating the bus collision. The helicopter, a Eurocopter AS350, went down near a large storage facility. At least four cars and two storage containers burned after the helicopter caught fire. NBC4 reporter Robert Kovacik was at the bus scene and saw black smoke and rushed to the helicopter crash site. Anchor and reporters pay tearful tributes to deceased colleagues Moreno was a familiar voice for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 during the station's aerial coverage. She and Marciniw were both were employees of Angel City Air, which operated the chopper for the station. Moreno, born in Orange County, joined Angel City Air in 2010, the same year she earned a broadcast journalism and political science degree from Chapman University. She reported for several news outlets and began flying with Marciniw in 2023, the NBC4 website said. Marciniw grew up in Southern California and graduated from Burbank High School in 1974. "I think a lot of us are still trying to process what happened, this terrible loss," NBC4 reporter Lauren Coronado told viewers early Wednesday as she stood near the crash site. A hazmat crew was cleaning up jet fuel, she said. In a tribute to Moreno and Marciniw, the newscast referred to them as "the team in the sky," saying Moreno would often post videos from her job and was in awe of the view. Anchor Lynette Romero held a colleague's hand and wiped away tears after hearing Moreno's voice when one of her posts was played. In an interview with the station, Esteban Jimenez, a pilot, said he had known Marciniw since the 1990s. He said Marciniw had been his instructor. "I just talked to him on Sunday. We were talking about the aviation business and retiring," he said. Expert talks about what may have caused the crash Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti said the alarm sounding in the helicopter's final video sounds like the low rotor RPM warning horn that signals the main rotor is no longer spinning enough to keep the helicopter in the air. "It just has all the earmarks of a potential loss of engine power and a dangerous decrease in the main rotor speed," said Guzzetti who used to investigate crashes for both the NTSB and FAA. Guzzetti said the pilot appeared to be trying to perform an emergency maneuver to use the wind to force the rotor to spin again much like a breeze turns a windmill. Doing that can create a bit of lift that could help cushion the impact, but Guzzetti said there would have been little opportunity to do that because the helicopter had been hovering at a low altitude beforehand. There are risks to news helicopters particularly in a major city like Los Angeles where multiple helicopters respond to an incident, but the pilots all coordinate closely over the radio to ensure they maintain a safe distance from each other. The industry also shares best practices to help keep these news flights safe. "It's a very unique form of flying. And the community is very good about lessons learned," Guzzetti said. "And so because of that, you don't hear about too many of those accidents. So they're rare, but they do occur, just because the mission is a risky one." Other crashes involving news helicopters The station said this is the second aviation tragedy in its history. In 1977, a KNBC news helicopter crashed when it ran out of fuel while returning to the station after covering a wildfire in Santa Barbara, killing the pilot and camera operator. The pilot, former U.S. Air Force officer Francis Gary Powers, had been in the news years earlier when he was shot down and captured while flying a U-2 spy plane over the Soviet Union for the CIA, an ordeal portrayed in the movie "Bridge of Spies." There have been at least eight fatal crashes involving news helicopters in the U.S. since 2000, killing 16 people, according to a review of federal accident records and news accounts. They include a 2023 crash in a New Jersey forest that killed the pilot and a photographer aboard a helicopter used by Philadelphia station WPVI, a 2022 crash beside a Charlotte, North Carolina, interstate that killed a pilot and meteorologist during a training flight for WBTV and the 2007 midair collision in Phoenix of two TV news helicopters that were covering a police chase. Golden reported from Seattle, and Collins from Hartford, Connecticut. Associated Press writers Josh Funk in Omaha, Nebraska; Olga Rodriguez in San Francisco; Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire; and Allen Breed in Raleigh, North Carolina, contributed. LOS ANGELES (NBC, KYMA) - Three people are dead and another is hospitalized after a helicopter crash in Chatsworth, California.
Nearly 60 firefighters responded to the crash just before 7 p.m. Tuesday on N. Mason Avenue in Chatsworth.
The helicopter went down between two commercial buildings, but firefighters say there was no exposure to any structures, and the fire has been completely extinguished.

6 dead in separate helicopter, bus crashes in Los Angeles
LOS ANGELES >> Three people were killed when an NBC4 news helicopter crashed and burst into flames Tuesday night in Chatsworth, not far from a serious accident involving a Metro bus that also left three people dead.
The area was already swarming with police, fire officials and the news media because of the bus crash when there was a fireball and people heard a loud explosion a few blocks away.
The chopper went down between two commercial buildings in the 9100 block of Mason Avenue around 7 p.m.
The LAFD said at least one person on the ground was killed. Two others were taken to a hospital.
KNBC said reporter Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw were killed.
NBC4 news anchor Colleen Williams confirmed around 9 p.m. that the station’s Chopper 4 had crashed. She had earlier told viewers that the station had lost contact with its team in the air.

“We are going to take a couple of minutes to think about that, to process, and to regroup,” Williams said before the station ended its live coverage.
Moreno and Marciniw’s last moments were tragically captured on a live broadcast. Video from their helicopter shows an aerial view of the bus crash, with the sound of the helicopter in the background.
Then, the sound of the engine’s motor winds down, the angle of the camera begins to descend, and Moreno is heard saying “You can’t pull up?” before the image cuts out.
Zoey Tur, a veteran news helicopter pilot who operated the type of helicopter the NBC4 crew was flying, said the aircraft has “an emergency horn that sounds when either there’s a low RPM issue or the helicopter loses hydraulics.”
“If you listen carefully to the on board transmission, the microphone picks up the engine shutting down,” Tur told The Times. “First, the engine starts winding down, which in turn reduces power to the router blades. Then you hear the horn warning of low rotor RPM. You can even hear the blade slap slow down.”
But, Tur pointed out, there was enough fuel on the helicopter to cause a fire, so why the rotors stopped spinning is currently unknown. Both the National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration are investigating.
Moreno “graduated from Chapman University with a degree in broadcast journalism and political science. She’d been flying in news choppers since the year 2010. George Marciniw, her helicopter pilot, grew up here in Southern California. He graduated from Burbank High School in 1974. They began flying together in 2023. George and Eliana often flew together, and you probably recall she often referred to him when they were covering stories together,” Williams said.
The helicopter crashed in a driveway between two warehouses, smashing into a pair of truck cargo containers. Four nearby vehicles also caught fire. Neither of the warehouse buildings were hit.
Woodland Hills resident Allyona Sevanesian said she and her husband were en route to a grocery store when she saw a cloud of smoke and they investigated “to make sure everybody was OK” but found a sobering scene.
“We drove there … behind the building,” the publicist said. “There was a gentleman that was hit by the helicopter.”
By 7:30 p.m., the flames were extinguished by police and fire crews at the scene.
Earlier in the evening, three people were killed and as many as six others injured when an SUV smashed into the side of a Metro bus in Chatsworth. The lodged vehicle trapped bus riders, who had to be extricated by first responders.
A Metro Line 166 bus was traveling eastbound on Nordhoff Street at 5:02 p.m. when it was hit by the SUV traveling southbound on De Soto Avenue, according to L.A. Metro.
Those injured in the bus crash were taken to a local hospital, according to Jennifer Middleton, a spokesperson for the Los Angeles Fire Department. No information was immediately available on the severity of the injuries. The Fire Department said it did not have a breakdown of how many of the eight people were in the bus or the SUV.
Soon after the wreck, local TV news video showed the front half of the SUV embedded in the side of the bus. Later, the vehicle was removed and a gaping hole was visible in the Metro bus’ side, with wreckage strewn around the scene. A white tent was erected nearby.
About 50 people, including families with young children, were gathered near the site of the bus crash late Tuesday.
“Anybody could be gone in a minute, you know?” said Winnetka resident Michael Sanchez, a physical therapist. When he learned of the tragedies, he decided, “let me go over there, look at the crash and say a couple of prayers.”
At a news conference around 9:45 p.m. near where the helicopter went down, Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass praised first responders who rushed to two “incredibly difficult” incidents within hours.
Los Angeles County Supervisor Lindsey Horvath, whose district includes the neighborhood of Chatsworth, also spoke, saying she wanted to “acknowledge just how many people are carrying this tragedy this evening. The riders who were on that bus, the Metro operator, and our bus operators across our system who mourn.”
“Members of our local news community who came here to do their jobs and experienced a profound tragedy of their own. This has been a deeply traumatic day for far too many people.”
More than 70 firefighters responded to the scene of the helicopter crash, according to LAFD Capt. Rico Gross. “We did have a loss of lives, three members of the community, and two members were transported to the hospital,” he said.
When NBC4 resumed its live coverage around 9:40 p.m., anchor Williams said the news station’s helicopter team had been out covering the bus crash. “We’re getting ready to go on the air with that … and we see this large plume of smoke, and realize something else has happened.
“Just a couple blocks away, our helicopter went down, it crashed,” she said.
NBC-TV Channel 4 and Telemundo’s KVEA-TV Channel 52 said in a statement late Tuesday, “We are deeply saddened to share that a helicopter providing aerial news coverage for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 was involved in a fatal accident in Los Angeles on Tuesday evening. We extend our heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives.”
The aviation tragedy was not the first that NBC4 had experienced.
In 1977, Francis Gary Powers was killed in a helicopter crash in Encino while working as a “Telecopter” reporter for KNBC.
Powers and a KNBC cameraman, George Spears, were returning from covering brushfires north of Santa Barbara when the helicopter Powers was piloting crashed into an open field near the Sepulveda Dam, carving a 21-foot-long gouge in the ground and killing both men.
According to The Times’ archives, Powers was a “conservative flier” who, on his final flight, ran out of fuel.
Powers was a figure in Cold War history. While employed as a U-2 spy-plane pilot for the CIA, Powers was shot down over the Soviet Union in 1960.
In 2000, a Fox 11 helicopter covering the Academy Awards crashed and burst into flames at Van Nuys Airport. The pilot reported mechanical difficulties moments before the crash in the southeast corner of the airport, The Times reported at the time. A television helicopter pilot from a competing station who overheard emergency radio transmissions from the helicopter said the craft was headed for the Shrine Auditorium just after 10 p.m. when the pilot reported a loss of hydraulic power.
In 2019, an ABC7 chopper was struck by an object believed to be a drone while flying over downtown Los Angeles. No one was hurt.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom posted: “Our hearts are with the victims and families of tonight’s devastating Metro bus and helicopter crashes in Chatsworth, and with the entire NBC4 family.”
The station was grieving the tragedy this morning.
“They were sacrificing their lives in service of their community,” NBC morning anchor Lynette Romero told viewers, with her co-anchors by her side. “They were determined and dedicated until the very end doing the job they loved so much. Our hearts are heavy this morning but we are here with you, we are here for you as we try to navigate these tragedies together.”
For reporters on the ground covering the bus crash, it was not immediately clear what happened when the chopper went down. First responders and reporters rushed to the scene and found the helicopter burning and a man injured nearby.

3 people killed when NBC and Telemundo news helicopter crashes while covering LA bus collision
LOS ANGELES (AP) — A news helicopter used by NBC and Telemundo crashed in a Los Angeles neighborhood and burst into flames, killing at least three people while reporters were covering the collision of an SUV and a city bus, officials and the news outlet said.
Colleen Williams, an NBC4 Los Angeles anchor, confirmed during live broadcasts that two people were killed Tuesday when the chopper went down. At least one other person was killed on the ground, a spokesperson for the Los Angeles Fire Department said.
“We are going to take a couple of minutes to think about that, process it,” Williams said, her voice shaking with emotion. Moments later the coverage cut off.
There were no immediate details on what may have caused the helicopter to crash.
The helicopter went down near a large storage facility in the neighborhood of Chatsworth in the San Fernando Valley, officials said. News crews were reporting on a collision from earlier in the day, when an SUV slammed into the middle of a city bus, killing at least two people and injuring six others. Photos and videos online showed half the SUV lodged in the side of the bus.
At least four cars and two storage containers on the ground burned after the helicopter caught fire, which was quickly put out, according to officials. NBC4 reporter Robert Kovacik was at the bus scene and saw black smoke and rushed to the helicopter crash site. Dozens of police cars surrounded the scene as ambulances entered.
Two people were brought to a hospital, said Rico A. Gross, a fire department battalion chief. Their conditions were not immediately released.
News station identifies those on the helicopter
Williams and the station’s website identified the dead aboard the helicopter as Eliana Moreno, a familiar voice for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 during the station’s aerial coverage, and pilot George Marciniw. Both were employees of Angel City Air, which operated the chopper.
Moreno, born in Orange County, joined the Angel City Air helicopter team in 2010, the same year she earned a broadcast journalism and political science degree from Chapman University. She reported for several Southern California news outlets and began flying with Marciniw in 2023, the NBC4 website said.
Marciniw grew up in Southern California and graduated from Burbank High School in 1974.
“I think a lot of us are still trying to process what happened, this terrible loss,” NBC4 reporter Lauren Coronado said during a newscast early Wednesday. She was standing near the crash site during the newscast and said a hazmat crew was cleaning up jet fuel.
In a tribute to Moreno and Marciniw, the newscast referred to them as “the team in the sky,” saying Moreno would often post videos from her job and was in awe of the view she had. News anchor Lynette Romero held a colleague’s hand and wiped away tears after hearing Moreno’s voice when one of her posts was played.
In an interview with the station, Esteban Jimenez, a pilot, said he had known Marciniw since the 1990s. He said Marciniw had been his instructor.
“I just talked to him on Sunday. We were talking about the aviation business and retiring,” he said.
Condolences for the victims and their families
NBC4 and Telemundo 52 Los Angeles said in a statement they “are deeply saddened” and extended “heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives.”
“Losing five Angelenos is very painful,” Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said. “And I know this community of Chatsworth, hit hard, will be grieving for some time.”
California Gov. Gavin Newsom thanked the emergency crews responding to both crashes and said in a post on X that “our hearts are with the victims and families.”
The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration said personnel will arrive Wednesday to begin an investigation into the cause of the helicopter crash.
There have been at least eight fatal crashes involving news helicopters in the U.S. since 2000, killing 16 people, according to a review of federal accident records and news accounts. They include a 2023 crash in a New Jersey forest that killed the pilot and a photographer aboard a helicopter used by Philadelphia station WPVI and a 2022 crash beside a Charlotte, North Carolina, interstate that killed a pilot and meteorologist during a training flight for WBTV.

Three people were killed Tuesday when a helicopter used by NBC4 Los Angeles and Telemundo 52 crashed and erupted in flames in the Chatsworth neighborhood while its crew was covering an earlier collision between an SUV and a Los Angeles city bus.
Two people aboard the helicopter — pilot George Marciniw and journalist Eliana Moreno — were killed, according to NBC4. The Los Angeles Fire Department said at least one additional person died on the ground.
The helicopter came down near a large storage facility in Chatsworth, part of the San Fernando Valley, igniting vehicles and storage containers as wreckage scattered across the area.
At least four cars and two storage containers caught fire following the crash. Firefighters quickly extinguished the flames, officials said.
The impact left the aircraft so badly damaged that emergency crews initially could not determine basic identifying features of the helicopter or immediately establish how many people had been aboard.
“From the helicopter itself, it’s pretty well destroyed,” Los Angeles Fire Department Capt. Branden Silverman said. “So we are going to have to go through the rubble and see how many victims there were on board, as well as identify the helicopter; we couldn’t even see a tail.”
Two additional people were transported to a hospital following the helicopter crash, according to Los Angeles Fire Department Battalion Chief Rico A. Gross. Their conditions were not immediately available.
NBC4 reporter Robert Kovacik was working at the scene of the bus collision when he noticed black smoke and headed toward the helicopter crash site. Dozens of police vehicles surrounded the area as ambulances moved into the scene.
NBC4 anchor Colleen Williams confirmed the deaths of the two people aboard the helicopter during the station’s live coverage.
“We are going to take a couple of minutes to think about that, process it,” Williams said, her voice shaking with emotion.
The broadcast cut away moments later.
NBC4 and Telemundo 52 subsequently identified the two crew members as Moreno and Marciniw, both employees of Angel City Air, the company operating the aircraft.
Moreno had become a familiar voice to viewers of NBC4 and Telemundo 52 through the stations’ aerial news coverage.
Born in Orange County, Moreno joined Angel City Air’s helicopter team in 2010. That same year, she graduated from Chapman University with degrees in broadcast journalism and political science.
She worked for several Southern California news organizations during her career and began flying with Marciniw in 2023, according to NBC4.
Marciniw was raised in Southern California and graduated from Burbank High School in 1974.
NBC4 and Telemundo 52 said they “are deeply saddened” by the deaths and extended “heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives.”
The helicopter crew had been covering another deadly incident when the aircraft went down.
Earlier Tuesday, an SUV crashed into the middle of a Los Angeles city bus, killing at least two people and injuring six others. Images and video from that scene showed a large portion of the SUV embedded in the side of the bus.
The two disasters left at least five people dead in Los Angeles on Tuesday — at least two in the vehicle-bus collision and three connected to the helicopter crash.
“Losing five Angelenos is very painful,” Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said. “And I know this community of Chatsworth, hit hard, will be grieving for some time.”
California Gov. Gavin Newsom thanked emergency personnel who responded to both scenes and said that “our hearts are with the victims and families.”
Federal investigators are now preparing to determine what caused the helicopter to go down.
The National Transportation Safety Board and Federal Aviation Administration said investigators would arrive Wednesday to begin examining the crash.
The investigation is expected to focus on the helicopter, its flight operations and other evidence necessary to establish what happened before the aircraft descended into the Chatsworth neighborhood.
Tuesday’s accident adds to a relatively small but deadly series of crashes involving U.S. news helicopters during the past quarter-century.
At least eight fatal accidents involving news helicopters have occurred in the United States since 2000, killing 16 people, according to a review of federal accident records and news reports.
Among them was a 2023 accident in a New Jersey forest involving a helicopter used by Philadelphia television station WPVI. The pilot and photographer aboard were killed.
A pilot and meteorologist working for WBTV were killed in 2022 when their helicopter crashed beside an interstate in Charlotte, North Carolina, during a training flight.
Tuesday’s Los Angeles crash occurred while Marciniw and Moreno were carrying out the same type of aerial newsgathering work, covering a deadly emergency elsewhere in the city when their helicopter went down and created a second fatal scene.

A co-anchor for NBC Los Angeles paid an emotional tribute to her two colleagues after they were among three people killed in a helicopter crash on Sept. 15, saying the duo “died doing what they loved.”

“They were both doing what they loved so much,” Romero said. “For me, that’s comfort in knowing how happy they were. They loved breaking news, and they loved being in NewsChopper 4.”
Eliana Moreno
Moreno graduated in 2010 from nearby Chapman University in Orange with a degree in broadcast journalism and political science, according to NBC Los Angeles.
She came from a big family who were “so proud of her” for “being on the news in her hometown,” according to Romero. She also was an animal lover who owned dogs and kept chickens, Romero said.
Moreno had reported for multiple outlets in Southern California after joining Angel City Air in 2010.
The bilingual reporter, who was in her 30s, had worked at NBC Los Angeles and Telemundo 52 for about a decade. She was engaged to be married, Romero said.

“I surpassed everything I thought I could ever do so let’s see what I do next!” she wrote.

Seven Republicans joined all Democrats in voting Tuesday night, passing the resolution 220 to 204.
That’s up from four Republicans who backed a similar House measure in July.
The resolution directs Trump to remove U.S. forces from hostilities with Iran unless Congress specifically authorizes them.
The vote comes as the war approaches seven months, far longer than Trump initially said the fighting would last. The measure would still need to clear the Senate, and it’s unclear whether the chamber will take it up.
A similar House resolution passed in July has yet to reach the Senate. Even if this one reaches the president’s desk, Trump is expected to veto it.
This is likely the House’s last vote on war powers on Iran before the midterms, but it may not be the last Iran-related vote before lawmakers leave Washington.
Massie moves to impeach Pete Hegseth
The House could vote as soon as Wednesday on a Republican effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., introduced the articles Tuesday. He has accused Hegseth of “high crimes and misdemeanors” over the Iran war and other military operations.
Massie spent hours on the House floor reading his 34-page resolution, arguing that Hegseth has abused the powers of his office.
“He will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law. Peter Bryan Hegseth thus warrants impeachment and trial. Removal from office and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust or profit under the United States.”
Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky
Massie has been among the most vocal Republican critics of the Iran war. He said he didn’t inform House leaders he was about to force this fight.
“I didn’t give anybody a heads-up,” Massie said. “When they found out I was doing the Epstein discharge petition, they canceled two weeks of Congress, and I think if they found out I was going to do this, they might have canceled even more days.”
Massie and Hegseth already have a history. Hegseth campaigned for Massie’s Republican primary opponent in May, and that opponent went on to defeat him.
The Trump administration continues to back Hegseth. Attorney General Todd Blanche said Hegseth “follows the law” and is doing a “phenomenal job.”
House leaders have to act on Massie’s resolution by Thursday, just before lawmakers leave Washington for an extended recess through the midterms.
Congress splits over new AI guardrails
People building some of the world’s most powerful AI systems warn that the technology is moving too fast and could eventually slip beyond human control. That warning has now reached Capitol Hill.
There’s a lot of talk about what to do, but so far, Congress hasn’t agreed on how far to go. The divide was on full display Tuesday.
Attorney General Todd Blanche sided with Trump, who has called fears of AI taking over the world a “hoax.” Blanche said the timing, two months before the midterms, is political.
“This should not be breaking news. That this AI issue, which suddenly came up two months before an election, is being discussed, and the president calls it a hoax. The way this has come around today, not three months ago, I mean, I was watching the news today, and every Democratic senator suddenly raced to a microphone to talk about AI after being eerily silent for months and months and months. So, to talk [about] the timing of this as being nothing but an effort to influence the midterms, I shouldn’t have to say that out loud.”
Todd Blanche, U.S. Attorney General
House Speaker Mike Johnson said Congress shouldn’t rush into new AI restrictions. But he is open to some guardrails, including independent audits and more transparency from the companies developing the technology. He also said Trump plans to bring top AI executives to the White House within the next week.
“They can self-police. They can self-regulate. They don’t need the government to tell them to slow it down; if they want to slow down, they should. But we cannot, we cannot have a moratorium on the development of AI because then we will lose our edge to China, and that has serious national security implications for every American family,” Johnson said.
Democratic senators have pressed Congress to move faster. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said lawmakers shouldn’t leave for another recess without acting.
“These new models are scary. We’re dealing here with real peril, not science fiction. And, so there should be an urgency. We should not break for any kind of recess without dealing with AI.
We’re way past trusting big tech; that era of voluntary self-regulation is gone. We need a regimen of oversight, much as we do with pharmaceutical drugs or other potential dangers. And we need to do it now.
When it comes to new technology, Congress is seldom ever in front of the parade, lagging far behind. And, so the president tells us, not to worry. That’s not enough.”
Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut
Some movement toward a middle ground exists. Senate Majority Leader John Thune says he wants a “light touch” that addresses the most serious AI threats without stifling development.
But so far, Congress hasn’t agreed on what that looks like or when it will act.
Kennedy Center closes for two-year renovation after judge blocks efforts to add Trump’s name
The Kennedy Center’s Trump-led board voted Tuesday to close the building for a two-year renovation. The center closed immediately after administrators warned that keeping it open could put lives at risk.
But Trump said the $250 million renovation won’t begin until an appeals court rules on the dispute over placing his name on the building.
A federal judge has blocked the name change, ruling that the board lacks the authority to rename the presidential memorial without Congress. Trump said he’ll appeal. If the courts ultimately rule against the center, he said the renovation won’t happen.
While that project is now on hold, another Trump project is complete. The president shared a photo of the new White House helipad, calling it a “work of art” and said it was completed ahead of schedule and under budget. It’s the latest in Trump’s broader makeover of the White House and its grounds.
Work also continues on the new ballroom, built on the site of the demolished East Wing. Trump has also pushed projects beyond the White House, including work around the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool and plans for a triumphal arch.
Corn mazes across 20 farms pay tribute to Dolly Parton’s legacy
Dolly Parton is once again larger than life, now featured in cornfields across the U.S. and Canada.
This fall, 20 farms have turned their cornfields into massive Dolly-themed mazes to celebrate her music, career and charitable efforts. The organizers selected Dolly for this year’s country music corn maze campaign months before her passing in August, turning the project into a tribute afterward.
Maize, a Utah-based company that designs farm attractions nationwide, crafted these mazes. Past honorees include Reba McEntire, Luke Bryan and Lainey Wilson.
At one Connecticut farm, five acres of corn have been shaped into Dolly’s likeness. But turning that famous look, specifically her hair, into a maze poses a particular challenge.
“She has a lot of it, and it comes to little tips, and you don’t know where the next little opening is going to be,” corn maze owner Danielle Gallop said.
Even in a cornfield, Dolly’s hair remains a complex feature to replicate.
This year’s mazes also give back, with part of the proceeds supporting Dolly’s Imagination Library. Visitors can enjoy Dolly trivia, photo opportunities and, most importantly, a map.
More from Straight Arrow:
Farm bankruptcies are up 46%. Can the family farm survive modern geopolitical shocks?
Wheat farmer Andy Juris finds his balance sheet agonizing.
The cost of necessities such as fertilizer zip along a continuous incline, while the price of wheat he grows in southern Washington State falls short of his expenses.
“A lot of the inflation that started post-COVID never really left agriculture,” Juris told Straight Arrow.
The price of diesel fuel, for example, hit a record high this month.
Juris’ farm is a short drive from the river that separates Washington from Oregon, where dried-out grass and wheat grow from level terrain bathed in the shadow of the Cascade Mountains. While western Washington is renowned for dense forests sustained by frequent rainfall and picturesque views of the Pacific Ocean, Juris said his part of the state is decidedly more desolate.
“We’re basically a desert that, in some places, doesn’t look any different than Death Valley,” he said.
The farmer grows dryland wheat, so named for its climate, and counts himself among the fortunate ones.

3 people killed when NBC and Telemundo news helicopter crashes while covering LA bus collision - Boston News, Weather, Sports
sources.text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — A news helicopter crashed in a Los Angeles neighborhood on Tuesday and burst into flames, killing at least three people while reporters were covering the collision of an SUV and a city bus, officials and the news outlet said.
Colleen Williams, an NBC4 Los Angeles anchor, confirmed during live broadcasts that two people were killed when the chopper went down. At least one other person was killed on the ground, a spokesperson for the Los Angeles Fire Department said.
“We are going to take a couple of minutes to think about that, process it,” Williams said, her voice shaking with emotion. Moments later the coverage cut off.
The helicopter, used by NBC and Telemundo, went down near a large storage facility in the neighborhood of Chatsworth in the San Fernando Valley, officials said. News crews were reporting on a collision from earlier in the day, when an SUV slammed into the middle of a city bus, killing at least two people and injuring six others. Photos and videos online showed half the SUV lodged in the side of the bus.
“From the helicopter itself, it’s pretty well destroyed,” Capt. Branden Silverman, a spokesperson for the fire department, said. “So we are going to have to go through the rubble and see how many victims there were on board, as well as identify the helicopter; we couldn’t even see a tail.”
At least four cars and two storage containers on the ground burned after the helicopter caught fire, which was quickly put out, according to officials. NBC4 reporter Robert Kovacik was at the bus scene and saw black smoke and rushed to the helicopter crash site. Dozens of police cars surrounded the scene as ambulances entered.
Two people were brought to a hospital, said Rico A. Gross, a fire department battalion chief. Their conditions were not immediately released.
Williams and the station’s website identified the dead aboard the helicopter as Eliana Moreno, a familiar voice for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 during the station’s aerial coverage, and pilot George Marciniw. Both were employees of Angel City Air, which operated the chopper.
Moreno, born in Orange County, joined the Angel City Air helicopter team in 2010, the same year she earned a broadcast journalism and political science degree from Chapman University. She reported for several Southern California news outlets and began flying with Marciniw in 2023, the NBC4 website said.
Marciniw grew up in Southern California and graduated from Burbank High School in 1974.
“Losing five Angelenos is very painful,” Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said. “And I know this community of Chatsworth, hit hard, will be grieving for some time.”
NBC4 and Telemundo 52 Los Angeles said in a statement they “are deeply saddened” and extended “heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives.”
Gov. Gavin Newsom thanked the emergency crews responding to both crashes and said in a post on X that “our hearts are with the victims and families.”
The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration said personnel will arrive Wednesday to begin an investigation into the cause of the helicopter crash.
There have been at least eight fatal crashes involving news helicopters in the U.S. since 2000, killing 16 people, according to a review of federal accident records and news accounts.
They include a 2023 crash in a New Jersey forest that killed the pilot and a photographer aboard a helicopter used by Philadelphia station WPVI and a 2022 crash beside a Charlotte, North Carolina, interstate that killed a pilot and meteorologist during a training flight for WBTV.

At least 6 dead in helicopter crash and bus accident in LA’s Chatsworth neighborhood. Driver arrested
LOS ANGELES — Three people were killed when an NBC4 news helicopter crashed and burst into flames Tuesday night in Chatsworth not far from a serious collision involving a Metro bus that also left three people dead.
The area was already swarming with police, fire officials and the news media because of the bus crash when there was a fireball and people heard a loud explosion a few blocks away.
The chopper went down between two commercial buildings in the 9100 block of Mason Avenue around 7 p.m.
The LAFD said at least one person on the ground was killed. Two others were taken to a hospital.
KNBC said reporter Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw were killed.
NBC4 news anchor Colleen Williams confirmed around 9 p.m. that the station’s Chopper 4 had crashed. She had earlier told viewers that the station had lost contact with its team in the air.
“We are going to take a couple of minutes to think about that, to process, and to regroup,” Williams said before the station ended its live coverage.
Moreno and Marciniw’s last moments tragically were captured on a live broadcast. Video from their helicopter shows an aerial view of the bus crash, with the sound of the helicopter in the background.
Then, the sound of the engine’s motor winds down, the angle of the camera begins to descend, and Moreno is heard saying “You can’t pull up?” before the image cuts out.
Zoey Tur, a veteran news helicopter pilot who operated the type of helicopter the NBC4 crew was flying, said the aircraft has “an emergency horn that sounds when either there’s a low RPM issue or the helicopter loses hydraulics.”
“If you listen carefully to the on board transmission, the microphone picks up the engine shutting down,” Tur told The Times. “First, the engine starts winding down, which in turn reduces power to the router blades. Then you hear the horn warning of low rotor RPM. You can even hear the blade slap slow down.”
But, Tur pointed out, there was enough fuel on the helicopter to cause a fire, so why the rotors stopped spinning is currently unknown. Both the National Transportation Safety Board and Federal Aviation Administration are investigating.
Moreno “graduated from Chapman University with a degree in broadcast journalism and political science. She’d been flying in news choppers since the year 2010. George Marciniw, her helicopter pilot, grew up here in Southern California. He graduated from Burbank High School in 1974. They began flying together in 2023. George and Eliana often flew together, and you probably recall she often referred to him when they were covering stories together,” Williams said.
The helicopter crashed in a driveway between two warehouses, smashing into a pair of truck cargo containers. Four nearby vehicles also caught fire. Neither of the warehouse buildings were hit.
Woodland Hills resident Allyona Sevanesian said she and her husband were en route to a grocery store when she saw a cloud of smoke and they investigated “to make sure everybody was OK” but found a sobering scene.
“We drove there … behind the building,” the publicist said. “There was a gentleman that was hit by the helicopter.”
By 7:30 p.m., the flames were extinguished by police and fire crews at the scene.
Earlier in the evening, three people were killed and as many as six others injured when an SUV smashed into the side of a Metro bus in Chatsworth. The lodged vehicle trapped bus riders, who had to be extricated by first responders.
A Metro Line 166 bus was traveling eastbound on Nordhoff Street at 5:02 p.m. when it was hit by the SUV traveling southbound on De Soto Avenue, according to L.A. Metro.
The SUV’s driver, Bailee Lynn Rios, 36, was booked on suspicion of murder in connection with the bus crash, according to the LAPD. She is being held in lieu of $4 million bail.
Those injured in the bus crash were taken to a local hospital, according to Jennifer Middleton, a spokesperson for the Los Angeles Fire Department. No information was immediately available on the severity of the injuries. The Fire Department said it did not have a breakdown of how many of the eight people were in the bus or the SUV.
Soon after the wreck, local TV news video showed the front half of the SUV embedded in the side of the bus. Later, the vehicle was removed and a gaping hole was visible in the Metro bus’ side, with wreckage strewn around the scene. A white tent was erected nearby.
About 50 people, including families with young children, were gathered near the site of the bus crash late Tuesday.
“Anybody could be gone in a minute, you know?” said Winnetka resident Michael Sanchez, a physical therapist. When he learned of the tragedies, he decided, “let me go over there, look at the crash and say a couple of prayers.”
At a news conference around 9:45 p.m. near where the helicopter went down, Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass praised first responders who rushed to two “incredibly difficult” incidents within hours.
Los Angeles County Supervisor Lindsey Horvath, whose district includes the neighborhood of Chatsworth, also spoke, saying she wanted to “acknowledge just how many people are carrying this tragedy this evening. The riders who were on that bus, the Metro operator, and our bus operators across our system who mourn.”
“Members of our local news community who came here to do their jobs and experienced a profound tragedy of their own. This has been a deeply traumatic day for far too many people.”
More than 70 firefighters responded to the scene of the helicopter crash, according to LAFD Capt. Rico Gross. “We did have a loss of lives, three members of the community, and two members were transported to the hospital,” he said.
When NBC4 resumed its live coverage around 9:40 p.m., anchor Williams said the news station’s helicopter team had been out covering the bus crash. “We’re getting ready to go on the air with that … and we see this large plume of smoke, and realize something else has happened.
“Just a couple blocks away, our helicopter went down, it crashed,” she said.
NBC-TV Channel 4 and Telemundo’s KVEA-TV Channel 52 said in a statement late Tuesday, “We are deeply saddened to share that a helicopter providing aerial news coverage for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 was involved in a fatal accident in Los Angeles on Tuesday evening. We extend our heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives.”
The aviation tragedy was not the first that NBC4 had experienced.
In 1977, Francis Gary Powers was killed in a helicopter crash in Encino while working as a “Telecopter” reporter for KNBC.
Powers and a KNBC cameraman, George Spears, were returning from covering brushfires north of Santa Barbara when the helicopter Powers was piloting crashed into an open field near the Sepulveda Dam, carving a 21-foot-long gouge in the ground and killing both men.
According to The Times’ archives, Powers was a “conservative flier” who, on his final flight, ran out of fuel.
Powers was a figure in Cold War history. While employed as a U-2 spy-plane pilot for the CIA, Powers was shot down over the Soviet Union in 1960.
In 2000, a Fox 11 helicopter covering the Academy Awards crashed and burst into flames at Van Nuys Airport. The pilot reported mechanical difficulties moments before the crash in the southeast corner of the airport, The Times reported at the time. A television helicopter pilot from a competing station who overheard emergency radio transmissions from the helicopter said the craft was headed for the Shrine Auditorium just after 10 p.m. when the pilot reported a loss of hydraulic power.
In 2019, an ABC7 chopper was struck by an object believed to be a drone while flying over downtown Los Angeles. No one was hurt.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom posted: “Our hearts are with the victims and families of tonight’s devastating Metro bus and helicopter crashes in Chatsworth, and with the entire NBC4 family.”
On Wednesday morning, the station was grieving the tragedy.
“They were sacrificing their lives in service of their community,” NBC morning anchor Lynette Romero told viewers, with her co-anchors by her side. “They were determined and dedicated until the very end doing the job they loved so much. Our hearts are heavy this morning but we are here with you, we are here for you as we try to navigate these tragedies together.”
For reporters on the ground covering the bus crash, it was not immediately clear what happened when the chopper went down. First responders and reporters rushed to the scene and found the helicopter burning and a man injured nearby.

sources.text:
A motorist was arrested on murder charges after authorities say she slammed her SUV into a city bus in Los Angeles, killing at least two people and injuring six others in a prelude to a second deadly tragedy: the fiery crash of a TV news helicopter that was covering the collision.
Bailee Lynn Rios, 36, of Simi Valley, was arrested Tuesday night and was being held at a Los Angeles jail with bail set at US$4-million, police said Wednesday. The case is under review by the district attorney’s office, which will decide whether to file the charges in court or pursue different ones. Information on a lawyer who could speak on her behalf was not immediately available.
The helicopter, which was used by NBC and Telemundo, crashed about two hours after police say Rios drove her 2004 Ford Expedition the wrong way down a busy avenue, ran a red light and struck a vehicle before hitting the bus. One passenger was fully ejected from the bus and another was partially ejected, police said.
Rios’ mother, Cindy Rios, said she was shocked and saddened by the string of events. She said she had not spoken to Bailee Lynn since her arrest and had not been contacted by law enforcement.
“It’s just horrible,” Cindy Rios told The Associated Press in a phone interview Wednesday. “The fact that my daughter was involved and was the cause of it is just extremely disturbing.”
“If anything, I’m sorry for the other families,” she added. “My daughter’s alive. People lost their lives.”
The two people who died in the bus crash were identified as Gage Weida, 31, and Daniel Castillo, 46, of Los Angeles. No city was given for Weida, but according to his Facebook page, he also lived in Los Angeles.
NBC4 Los Angeles reported that two people aboard the helicopter – reporter Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw – were killed when the chopper went down Tuesday in the Chatsworth neighbourhood in the San Fernando Valley north of downtown. A person on the ground, identified as 29-year-old Edy Gutierrez Mejia, died in a parking lot, the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner’s Office said. He was from Guatemala, the country’s consulate confirmed.
The crash happened as news crews were reporting on the collision involving the SUV that slammed into the bus.
There were no immediate details on what caused the helicopter crash, but an alarm could be heard sounding inside the helicopter’s cockpit as it lost altitude in the final seconds of video the crew broadcast before the crash.
Just after the beeping noise starts, a woman’s voice says “uh oh.” The helicopter moves quickly away from the bus crash site and starts losing altitude. The woman says “You can’t pull up?” before the video stops as the chopper nears the ground.
“That video is probably the most important evidence that we have discovered so far,” National Transportation Safety Board investigator Fabian Salazar said Wednesday at a news briefing.
Salazar said the sounds were consistent with the helicopter’s engine changing speed, as well as what he said were likely advisory tones for the pilot. The NTSB said it is also investigating the bus collision.
The helicopter, a Eurocopter AS350, went down near a large storage facility. At least four cars and two storage containers burned after the helicopter caught fire. NBC4 reporter Robert Kovacik was at the bus scene and saw black smoke and rushed to the helicopter crash site.
The Associated Press
Moreno was a familiar voice for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 during the station’s aerial coverage. She and Marciniw were both were employees of Angel City Air, which operated the chopper for the station.
Moreno, born in Orange County, joined Angel City Air in 2010, the same year she earned a broadcast journalism and political science degree from Chapman University. She reported for several news outlets and began flying with Marciniw in 2023, the NBC4 website said.
Marciniw grew up in Southern California and graduated from Burbank High School in 1974.
“I think a lot of us are still trying to process what happened, this terrible loss,” NBC4 reporter Lauren Coronado told viewers early Wednesday as she stood near the crash site. A hazmat crew was cleaning up jet fuel, she said.
In a tribute to Moreno and Marciniw, the newscast referred to them as “the team in the sky,” saying Moreno would often post videos from her job and was in awe of the view. Anchor Lynette Romero held a colleague’s hand and wiped away tears after hearing Moreno’s voice when one of her posts was played.
In an interview with the station, Esteban Jimenez, a pilot, said he had known Marciniw since the 1990s. He said Marciniw had been his instructor.
“I just talked to him on Sunday. We were talking about the aviation business and retiring,” he said.
Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti said the alarm sounding in the helicopter’s final video sounds like the low rotor RPM warning horn that signals the main rotor is no longer spinning enough to keep the helicopter in the air.
“It just has all the earmarks of a potential loss of engine power and a dangerous decrease in the main rotor speed,” said Guzzetti who used to investigate crashes for both the NTSB and FAA.
Guzzetti said the pilot appeared to be trying to perform an emergency manoeuvre to use the wind to force the rotor to spin again much like a breeze turns a windmill. Doing that can create a bit of lift that could help cushion the impact, but Guzzetti said there would have been little opportunity to do that because the helicopter had been hovering at a low altitude beforehand.
There are risks to news helicopters particularly in a major city like Los Angeles where multiple helicopters respond to an incident, but the pilots all co-ordinate closely over the radio to ensure they maintain a safe distance from each other. The industry also shares best practices to help keep these news flights safe.
“It’s a very unique form of flying. And the community is very good about lessons learned,” Guzzetti said. “And so because of that, you don’t hear about too many of those accidents. So they’re rare, but they do occur, just because the mission is a risky one.”
The station said this is the second aviation tragedy in its history.
In 1977, a KNBC news helicopter crashed when it ran out of fuel while returning to the station after covering a wildfire in Santa Barbara, killing the pilot and camera operator. The pilot, former U.S. Air Force officer Francis Gary Powers, had been in the news years earlier when he was shot down and captured while flying a U-2 spy plane over the Soviet Union for the CIA, an ordeal portrayed in the movie Bridge of Spies.
There have been at least eight fatal crashes involving news helicopters in the U.S. since 2000, killing 16 people, according to a review of federal accident records and news accounts.
They include a 2023 crash in a New Jersey forest that killed the pilot and a photographer aboard a helicopter used by Philadelphia station WPVI and a 2022 crash beside a Charlotte, North Carolina, interstate that killed a pilot and meteorologist during a training flight for WBTV. A 2007 midair collision in Phoenix of two TV news helicopters that were covering a police chase led the NTSB to recommend that news helicopters have at least two people in the cockpit so the pilot can focus on flying while the reporter focuses on the story.

sources.text:
A helicopter providing news coverage of a bus collision in Los Angeles crashed, killing a journalist, the pilot and a person on the ground, broadcasters and authorities said.
No cause was given for the helicopter crash in the city's Chatsworth area, which came after a Metro bus collided with another vehicle earlier in the day, killing at least two people.
"We are deeply saddened to share that a helicopter providing aerial news coverage for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 was involved in a fatal accident in Los Angeles on Tuesday evening," NBC4 and Telemundo 52 said in a joint statement.
"We extend our heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives."
Parent company NBC News identified two of the victims as employees of helicopter operator Angel City Air: Eliana Moreno, who was also a photojournalist, and George Marciniw, the pilot.
One person also died outside the helicopter which was badly damaged, Los Angeles Fire Department said.
The crash was announced on air by NBC4.
"We knew we'd lost contact with our people out there, and we've just received the confirmation that, in fact, NewsChopper4 went down just before 7 o'clock tonight in Chatsworth," NBC anchor Colleen Williams said during an emotional live broadcast.
Two other people were taken to hospital, the fire service said. More than 70 firefighters responded to the crash, quickly putting out a fire at the scene.
"Our hearts are with the victims and families of tonight's devastating Metro bus and helicopter crashes in Chatsworth, and with the entire NBC4 family," said California Governor Gavin Newsom.

sources.news_title: Three killed after KNBC-TV helicopter crashes in Los Angeles suburb
sources.text:
Three people were killed when a helicopter used by a Los Angeles television station crashed while covering a news story there.
The crash occurred around 7 p.m. local time (10 p.m. Eastern Time) in Chatsworth, a neighborhood in northwestern Los Angeles.
Pilot George Maciniw and journalist Eliana Moreno were on board the helicopter at the time of the incident. Both were employed by Angel City Air, which provides aerial news gathering services to KNBC-TV (Channel 4) and KVEA (Channel 52, Telemundo).
Watch the initial moments when KNBC-TV learned a news helicopter crashed in a suburban Los Angeles neighborhood. At the time, its news team did not know that the helicopter belonged to their station. [Video: KNBC]
Full story: https://t.co/TLTWVy5eUx pic.twitter.com/C7STw2XvrG
The helicopter was in the air for about an hour, covering a fatal collision involving a Los Angeles municipal bus and a sports utility vehicle, when the aircraft experienced some kind of mechanical issue.
Video footage reviewed by The Desk revealed multiple alarms sounded in the helicopter about 10 seconds before it plummeted to the ground. Maciniw and Moreno were killed in the crash, as was an unidentified pedestrian who was on the ground, according to local officials.
KNBC confirmed its helicopter was involved in the crash in a statement broadcast around 9 p.m. local time; two hours later, the news outlet affirmed Maciniw and Moreno were on board the aircraft.
The last few minutes of KNBC-TV's helicopter flight was captured on live video transmissions sent back to the station. These were the final moments of that flight; conditions of those on board still unknown. 
Details here: https://t.co/CHA5cIVhEe pic.twitter.com/6mIST13BzK
The cause of the crash was not immediately clear. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) and the Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) are investigating the incident.
“We are deeply saddened to share that a helicopter providing aerial news coverage for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 was involved in a fatal accident in Los Angeles on Tuesday evening,” officials at KNBC and KVEA said in a statement. “We extend our heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives.”
On Tuesday, California Governor Gavin Newsom released a statement of condolences to the victims of the bus and helicopter crashes.
“Our hearts are with the victims and families of tonight’s devastating Metro bus and helicopter crashes in Chatsworth, and with the entire NBC4 family,” Newsom wrote on social media. “Thank you to the first responders working tirelessly tonight.”
Once common in the local television industry, news helicopters have been phased out in some smaller and medium-sized markets as costs to maintain a full-time pilot, photojournalist and mechanic can exceed more than $100,000 per month.
News helicopters are more common in major markets like Los Angeles and New York, where local TV stations either pool resources to provide aerial news coverage or have larger budgets to maintain them.
Helicopter used by news organizations are heavily regulated by strict rules, including requirements involving annual maintenance and preflight safety checks, according to one aviation expert who spoke with The Desk late Tuesday evening. Aircraft used by news organizations in California are also bound by state labor laws that limit the number of hours a pilot can fly.
The crash involving KNBC’s helicopter is the deadliest incident involving a newsgathering aircraft in three years. In December 2023, a news helicopter used by Philadelphia TV station WPVI (Channel 6, ABC) crashed while returning from a news story in New Jersey.
In Los Angeles, an aircraft used by KTLA (Channel 5) made an unscheduled landing in a parking lot after another pilot spotted white smoke coming from its engine bay. The cause of the smoke was determined to be a clogged oil line; no one was hurt in that incident.
KNBC and KVEA are part of NBC Universal, which is owned by Comcast.

An NBC news television helicopter crashed into a car park in Los Angeles on Tuesday, killing at least three people.
The helicopter crashed near a storage building in the neighbourhood of Chatsworth in the San Fernando Valley, as news crews were covering the bus crash that left at least two people dead and six others injured, according to the Los Angeles Fire Department. A fourth person was taken to hospital, though their condition was unknown.

“We are going to take a couple of minutes to think about that and process it,” she said, her voice shaking with emotion. Moments later, coverage was abruptly cut off.
The Los Angeles Fire Department said it was still working to determine how many of the victims had been on board the aircraft.
At least one person killed was on the ground outside, spokesperson Captain Branden Silverman told reporters.
"We're trying to determine how many patients were inside the helicopter," Silverman said.
The crash occurred near the scene of a separate deadly bus accident, though the connection between the two incidents, if any, was not immediately clear.
Photos and videos online showed around half of an SUV lodged into the side of an MTA bus and a large group of fire crew working around the crash.
Two people were reportedly killed and six others were injured after an SUV crashed into a city bus in Los Angeles, officials said.
According to the fire department, more than 50 firefighters responded to the helicopter crash. The fire had damaged four vehicles and two storage containers but was out by Tuesday evening, according to officials.
Silverman described the helicopter as “pretty well destroyed” and said they’re going to have to go through the rubble to see how many victims were on board.
According to media reports, the helicopter came down into a park serving a large single-storey building, striking or landing near several parked vehicles.
The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration will be handling the investigation.

sources.news_title: Helicopter Crash in Los Angeles Kills Three People, Injures One
sources.text:
(Bloomberg) -- Three people were killed and one injured when a helicopter crashed between two commercial buildings in the Chatsworth neighborhood of Los Angeles, the Los Angeles Fire Department said.
Four patients were assessed at the scene, three of whom were pronounced dead, according to the department. The fourth was taken to a local hospital in unknown condition.
One of those killed was a pedestrian in a parking lot, LAFD Fire Captain Branden Silverman said. The person was pulled by police officers from the fire area, and pronounced dead by paramedics.
It wasn’t immediately clear how many people were aboard the helicopter or whether anyone else killed was on the ground.
The crash came hours after three people were killed and six others injured when a sport utility vehicle struck the side of a Metro bus in Chatsworth, which is in the San Fernando Valley, north of central Los Angeles. The LAFD said it was unclear whether the helicopter was connected to the bus crash.
The first crew to arrive reported the helicopter down between the buildings, with fire from the crash spreading to four vehicles, the LAFD said. Fifty-six firefighters responded and later extinguished the fire, with no structures exposed. Four automobiles and two storage containers were damaged.
The helicopter was engulfed in flames when crews arrived, Silverman said at an earlier briefing, when searchers were still going through the wreckage.
The make and type of the helicopter weren’t known, and it was unclear where the aircraft had come from, according to the LAFD.
Silverman also declined to say whether the aircraft was a news helicopter.
“I don’t want to speculate that it’s a news helicopter because we have not confirmed that yet,” he said.
The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration will handle the investigation.
