sources.news_title: News Helicopter Crashes Covering LA Crash, Killing 3
sources.text:
A television news helicopter crashed and burst into flames in the Chatsworth neighborhood of Los Angeles' San Fernando Valley on Tuesday evening while covering a separate fatal collision between a Metro bus and an SUV nearby, killing three people and injuring a fourth, fire officials said. The Los Angeles Fire Department said the crash was reported just before 7 p.m. on the 9100 block of North Mason Avenue, with the aircraft coming down between two commercial buildings; the helicopter and nearby vehicles on the ground were engulfed in flames by the time firefighters arrived. Three people were pronounced dead at the scene, and a fourth was taken to a hospital in unknown condition. An LAFD spokesperson said one of those killed appeared to have been a pedestrian in a nearby parking lot. The identities of those killed had not been released by Tuesday night.
The helicopter, identified by NBC Los Angeles as its aircraft known on air as NewsChopper4, belonged to KNBC, the network's local affiliate. It had been recording footage of the earlier crash roughly two miles away, and NBC Los Angeles confirmed the downed aircraft was a news helicopter shortly after the incident, noting that several television news helicopters were operating in the same part of the west San Fernando Valley to cover the bus collision. The station's live broadcast showed the helicopter descending before its video feed abruptly cut off; anchors on air said afterward they were having difficulty reaching their colleagues. The cause of the crash was not immediately known, and NBC Los Angeles's own initial reporting characterized it only as unclear. The National Transportation Safety Board and Federal Aviation Administration will lead the investigation, a process that typically takes months to produce even a preliminary finding and considerably longer for a final determination of probable cause.
The crash the helicopter had been covering was reported roughly two hours earlier, at 5:03 p.m., when a Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority bus collided with an SUV on West Nordhoff Street in the same Chatsworth neighborhood. The Fire Department said the first crews to arrive found numerous injured people aboard the bus and worked to extricate those trapped inside. Local station KABC reported, citing sources, that at least two people died in that collision and eight others were injured, ranging from critical to minor. The SUV's driver was the vehicle's only occupant; that person's condition was not immediately known. Aerial footage taken before the helicopter crash showed the SUV heavily damaged against the side of the bus near a crosswalk, with firefighters working around both vehicles.
Tuesday's crash is not the first time a KNBC news helicopter has gone down while covering a story in the same general area. On Aug. 1, 1977, the station's helicopter, a Bell 206B JetRanger known as the "Telecopter," crashed in the Sepulveda Basin near Van Nuys Airport, about seven miles from Tuesday's crash site, killing pilot Francis Gary Powers and cameraman George Spears. Powers, who piloted the aircraft, was the former U-2 spy plane pilot whose plane was shot down over the Soviet Union in 1960, leading to his capture and a highly publicized Cold War prisoner exchange; he had gone on to work as a helicopter pilot and reporter for KNBC. Powers and Spears were returning to the station's Burbank heliport after covering the aftermath of a wildfire in Santa Barbara County when their aircraft went down.
News helicopter crashes, while uncommon relative to the volume of daily aerial coverage in major media markets, have recurred periodically across the industry. In April 2022, a helicopter operated for Philadelphia's WPVI-TV crashed in a wooded section of New Jersey's Wharton State Forest while returning from a Jersey Shore assignment, killing pilot Monroe Smith and photographer Christopher Dougherty; the aircraft was leased from a North Carolina-based operator and the FAA investigated that crash as well. Los Angeles is among a small number of U.S. media markets where multiple television stations maintain their own helicopters for live aerial coverage of breaking news, a practice that provides viewers with real-time video of unfolding incidents, including car chases, wildfires and traffic collisions, but that has occasionally drawn scrutiny over the safety and airspace-management challenges of concentrating several aircraft above a single active scene, as was reportedly the case Tuesday.
Investigators will need to determine whether mechanical failure, a midair collision with another aircraft, weather conditions, or another factor caused NewsChopper4 to go down, a question complicated by the number of press helicopters reported to have been operating in the same airspace at the time to cover the bus crash. The FAA maintains separate protocols for coordinating multiple aircraft over breaking news scenes in major markets, though the specifics of how those protocols applied Tuesday evening were not immediately available. Southern California's television stations have operated aerial news units for decades, a practice that traces back to KTLA's pioneering use of helicopter coverage in the 1950s and that both KNBC and its competitors have continued as a defining feature of Los Angeles television news.
Tuesday's events left two separate fatal incidents unfolding within the same neighborhood in the span of roughly two hours, compounding what began as a single traffic collision into a broader emergency response spanning both a roadway and a nearby commercial block. The Los Angeles Fire Department did not immediately say whether its response to the bus crash was affected by the subsequent helicopter crash occurring nearby, or whether resources had to be divided between the two scenes.

Moreno, born in Orange County, joined Angel City Air in 2010, the same year she earned a broadcast journalism and political science degree from Chapman University. She reported for several news outlets and began flying with Marciniw in 2023, the NBC4 website said.
Marciniw grew up in Southern California and graduated from Burbank High School in 1974.
“I think a lot of us are still trying to process what happened, this terrible loss,” NBC4 reporter Lauren Coronado told viewers early Wednesday as she stood near the crash site. A hazmat crew was cleaning up jet fuel, she said.
In a tribute to Moreno and Marciniw, the newscast referred to them as “the team in the sky,” saying Moreno would often post videos from her job and was in awe of the view. Anchor Lynette Romero held a colleague’s hand and wiped away tears after hearing Moreno’s voice when one of her posts was played.
In an interview with the station, Esteban Jimenez, a pilot, said he had known Marciniw since the 1990s. He said Marciniw had been his instructor.
“I just talked to him on Sunday. We were talking about the aviation business and retiring,” he said.
Expert talks about what may have caused the crash
Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti said the alarm sounding in the helicopter’s final video sounds like the low rotor RPM warning horn that signals the main rotor is no longer spinning enough to keep the helicopter in the air.
“It just has all the earmarks of a potential loss of engine power and a dangerous decrease in the main rotor speed,” said Guzzetti who used to investigate crashes for both the NTSB and FAA.
Guzzetti said the pilot appeared to be trying to perform an emergency maneuver to use the wind to force the rotor to spin again much like a breeze turns a windmill. Doing that can create a bit of lift that could help cushion the impact, but Guzzetti said there would have been little opportunity to do that because the helicopter had been hovering at a low altitude beforehand.
There are risks to news helicopters particularly in a major city like Los Angeles where multiple helicopters respond to an incident, but the pilots all coordinate closely over the radio to ensure they maintain a safe distance from each other. The industry also shares best practices to help keep these news flights safe.
“It’s a very unique form of flying. And the community is very good about lessons learned,” Guzzetti said. “And so because of that, you don’t hear about too many of those accidents. So they’re rare, but they do occur, just because the mission is a risky one.”
The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration said personnel would arrive Wednesday to begin an investigation into the cause of the helicopter crash.
Other crashes involving news helicopters
The station said this is the second aviation tragedy in its history.
In 1977, a KNBC news helicopter crashed when it ran out of fuel while returning to the station after covering a wildfire in Santa Barbara, killing the pilot and camera operator. The pilot, former U.S. Air Force officer Francis Gary Powers, had been in the news years earlier when he was shot down and captured while flying a U-2 spy plane over the Soviet Union for the CIA, an ordeal portrayed in the movie “Bridge of Spies.”
There have been at least eight fatal crashes involving news helicopters in the U.S. since 2000, killing 16 people, according to a review of federal accident records and news accounts. They include a 2023 crash in a New Jersey forest that killed the pilot and a photographer aboard a helicopter used by Philadelphia station WPVI and a 2022 crash beside a Charlotte, North Carolina, interstate that killed a pilot and meteorologist during a training flight for WBTV.
___
This story has been updated to correct that Marciniw, not Moreno, graduated from Burbank High School and to correct the spelling of Jeff Guzzetti’s last name.
___
Golden reported from Seattle and Collins reported from Hartford, Connecticut. Associated Press writers Josh Funk in Omaha, Nebraska; Olga Rodriguez in San Francisco; Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire; and Allen Breed in Raleigh, North Carolina; contributed to this report.

LOS ANGELES — The three victims of the deadly helicopter crash Tuesday evening have been identified by the Los Angeles County medical examiner's office.
The crash of NewsChopper4 occurred just before 7 p.m. between two commercial buildings at 9151 Mason Ave., near Nordhoff Street, the LA Fire Department reported.
Reporter Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw were killed aboard the helicopter, which is operated by Angel City Air and provided news coverage for NBC4 and its Spanish-language sister station, Telemundo 52, NBC4 announced.
The third person who died was identified as a 29-year-old man. Edy Gutierrez Mejia is believed to be the person who died on the ground in the business parking lot near where the chopper crash occurred.
A National Transportation Safety Board investigative team, along with the Federal Aviation Administration, was expected Wednesday in Chatsworth to begin trying to determine the cause of the crash that also injured two others.
Moreno was born in Orange County and graduated from Chapman University in 2010.
Marciniw grew up in Southern California, graduating from Burbank High School in 1974.
They began flying together in 2023.
"We are deeply saddened to share that a helicopter providing aerial news coverage for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 was involved in a fatal accident in Los Angeles on Tuesday evening," NBC4 and Telemundo 52 Los Angeles said in a statement. "We extend our heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives"
Moreno and Marciniw were covering the collision between an SUV and Metro bus that left three dead near the site of the helicopter crash.
A worker at a warehouse near the site of the helicopter crash who was in the parking lot at the time of the crash, was taken to a hospital. He was "shaken up more emotionally than physically," according to "LA Live News Tonight."
The helicopter crash ignited a fire exposing four vehicles, said Jennifer Middleton of the LAFD. The fire was extinguished.
Four automobiles and two storage containers were damaged by the fire, Middleton said.
"I'm absolutely devastated by the loss of life in Chatsworth tonight," Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said in a statement shared on social media. "My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we lost in the tragic bus collision and helicopter crash.
"I'm grateful to the City teams who responded so quickly. Please stay clear of the area as public safety officials remain on scene."
Supervisor Lindsey Horvath, whose Third District includes Chatsworth, said she is working with local authorities to understand what happened.
"I'm heartbroken by the devastating crash in Chatsworth. My thoughts are first and foremost with those who lost their lives, their families and loved ones, and everyone who was injured," she said.
"My office is in close contact with local authorities and Metro as we work to understand what happened and ensure those affected have the support they need. Thank you to the first responders who rushed to the scene and are caring for those in need."
Supervisor Kathryn Barger said the crash left her "shocked."
"I am shocked and deeply saddened by today's tragic helicopter crash involving members of the NBC4 family," said Barger, whose Fifth District includes Universal City, where NBC4 and Telemundo 52 are based.
"My heart goes out to everyone affected by this devastating loss, especially the families, friends, and colleagues of those who lost their lives. I extend my deepest condolences to the entire NBC4 community during this incredibly difficult time."

Powers was captured and sentenced to 10 years in a Soviet prison for espionage. He served 21 months of his sentence before being released in a prisoner swap in 1962.

sources.news_title: Three Dead after News Chopper Crashes near Bus Wreck in Los Angeles
sources.text:
Update: Final Moments of News Helicopter Captured Before Fatal Crash
Los Angeles Times
(TNS)
LOS ANGELES — Three people were killed when an NBC4 news helicopter crashed and burst into flames Tuesday night in Chatsworth not far from a serious collision involving a Metro bus that also left two people dead.
The area was already swarming with police, fire officials and the news media because of the bus crash when there was a fireball and people heard a loud explosion a few blocks away.
The chopper went down between two commercial buildings in the 9100 block of Mason Avenue around 7 p.m.
Two others were taken to a hospital.
KNBC said reporter Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw were killed.
NBC4 news anchor Colleen Williams confirmed around 9 p.m. that the station’s Chopper 4 had crashed. She had earlier told viewers that the station had lost contact with its team in the air.
“We are going to take a couple of minutes to think about that, to process, and to regroup,” Williams said before the station ended its live coverage.
Moreno and Marciniw’s last moments tragically were captured on a live broadcast. Video from their helicopter shows an aerial view of the bus crash, with the sound of the helicopter in the background.
Then, the sound of the engine’s motor winds down, the angle of the camera begins to descend, and Moreno is heard saying “You can’t pull up?” before the image cuts out.
Zoey Tur, a veteran news helicopter pilot who operated the type of helicopter the NBC4 crew was flying, said the aircraft has “an emergency horn that sounds when either there’s a low RPM issue or the helicopter loses hydraulics.”
“If you listen carefully to the on board transmission, the microphone picks up the engine shutting down,” Tur told the Los Angeles Times. “First, the engine starts winding down, which in turn reduces power to the rotor blades. Then you hear the horn warning of low rotor RPM. You can even hear the blade slap slow down.”
But, Tur pointed out, there was enough fuel on the helicopter to cause a fire, so why the rotors stopped spinning is currently unknown. Both the National Transportation Safety Board and Federal Aviation Administration are investigating.
Moreno “graduated from Chapman University with a degree in broadcast journalism and political science. She’d been flying in news choppers since the year 2010. George Marciniw, her helicopter pilot, grew up here in Southern California. He graduated from Burbank High School in 1974. They began flying together in 2023. George and Eliana often flew together, and you probably recall she often referred to him when they were covering stories together,” Williams said.
The helicopter crashed in a driveway between two warehouses, smashing into a pair of truck cargo containers. Four nearby vehicles also caught fire. Neither of the warehouse buildings were hit.
Woodland Hills resident Allyona Sevanesian said she and her husband were en route to a grocery store when she saw a cloud of smoke and they investigated “to make sure everybody was OK” but found a sobering scene.
“We drove there ... behind the building,” the publicist said. “There was a gentleman that was hit by the helicopter.”
By 7:30 p.m., the flames were extinguished by police and fire crews at the scene.
Earlier in the evening, two people were killed and as many as six others injured when an SUV smashed into the side of a Metro bus in Chatsworth. The lodged vehicle trapped bus riders, who had to be extricated by first responders.
A Metro Line 166 bus was traveling eastbound on Nordhoff Street at 5:02 p.m. when it was hit by the SUV traveling southbound on De Soto Avenue, according to L.A. Metro.
The SUV’s driver, Bailee Lynn Rios, 36, was booked on suspicion of murder in connection with the bus crash, according to the LAPD. She is being held in lieu of $4 million bail.
Gage Weida, 31, and Daniel Castillo, 46, of Arleta were identified Wednesday as the two killed in the bus crash, according to the Los Angeles County medical examiner’s office.
Those injured in the bus crash were taken to a local hospital, according to Jennifer Middleton, a spokesperson for the Los Angeles Fire Department. No information was immediately available on the severity of the injuries. The Fire Department said it did not have a breakdown of how many of the eight people were in the bus or the SUV.
Soon after the wreck, local TV news video showed the front half of the SUV embedded in the side of the bus. Later, the vehicle was removed and a gaping hole was visible in the Metro bus’ side, with wreckage strewn around the scene. A white tent was erected nearby.
About 50 people, including families with young children, were gathered near the site of the bus crash late Tuesday.
“Anybody could be gone in a minute, you know?” said Winnetka resident Michael Sanchez, a physical therapist. When he learned of the tragedies, he decided, “let me go over there, look at the crash and say a couple of prayers.”
At a news conference around 9:45 p.m. near where the helicopter went down, Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass praised first responders who rushed to two “incredibly difficult” incidents within hours.
Los Angeles County Supervisor Lindsey Horvath, whose district includes the neighborhood of Chatsworth, also spoke, saying she wanted to “acknowledge just how many people are carrying this tragedy this evening. The riders who were on that bus, the Metro operator, and our bus operators across our system who mourn.”
“Members of our local news community who came here to do their jobs and experienced a profound tragedy of their own. This has been a deeply traumatic day for far too many people.”
More than 70 firefighters responded to the scene of the helicopter crash, according to LAFD Capt. Rico Gross. “We did have a loss of lives, three members of the community, and two members were transported to the hospital,” he said.
When NBC4 resumed its live coverage around 9:40 p.m., anchor Williams said the news station’s helicopter team had been out covering the bus crash. “We’re getting ready to go on the air with that ... and we see this large plume of smoke, and realize something else has happened.
“Just a couple blocks away, our helicopter went down, it crashed,” she said.
NBC-TV Channel 4 and Telemundo’s KVEA-TV Channel 52 said in a statement late Tuesday, “We are deeply saddened to share that a helicopter providing aerial news coverage for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 was involved in a fatal accident in Los Angeles on Tuesday evening. We extend our heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives.”
The aviation tragedy was not the first that NBC4 had experienced.
In 1977, Francis Gary Powers was killed in a helicopter crash in Encino while working as a “Telecopter” reporter for KNBC.
Powers and a KNBC cameraman, George Spears, were returning from covering brushfires north of Santa Barbara when the helicopter Powers was piloting crashed into an open field near the Sepulveda Dam, carving a 21-foot-long gouge in the ground and killing both men.
According to the Times’ archives, Powers was a “conservative flier” who, on his final flight, ran out of fuel.
Powers was a figure in Cold War history. While employed as a U-2 spy-plane pilot for the CIA, Powers was shot down over the Soviet Union in 1960.
In 2000, a Fox 11 helicopter covering the Academy Awards crashed and burst into flames at Van Nuys Airport. The pilot reported mechanical difficulties moments before the crash in the southeast corner of the airport, the Times reported at the time. A television helicopter pilot from a competing station who overheard emergency radio transmissions from the helicopter said the craft was headed for the Shrine Auditorium just after 10 p.m. when the pilot reported a loss of hydraulic power.
In 2019, an ABC7 chopper was struck by an object believed to be a drone while flying over downtown Los Angeles. No one was hurt.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom posted: “Our hearts are with the victims and families of tonight’s devastating Metro bus and helicopter crashes in Chatsworth, and with the entire NBC4 family.”
On Wednesday morning, the station was grieving the tragedy.
“They were sacrificing their lives in service of their community,” NBC morning anchor Lynette Romero told viewers, with her co-anchors by her side. “They were determined and dedicated until the very end doing the job they loved so much. Our hearts are heavy this morning but we are here with you, we are here for you as we try to navigate these tragedies together.”
For reporters on the ground covering the bus crash, it was not immediately clear what happened when the chopper went down. First responders and reporters rushed to the scene and found the helicopter burning and a man injured nearby.
_____
(Los Angeles Times staff writers Meg James, Jasmine Mendez and Hannah Fry contributed to this report.)

By: Nana Karikari, Senior Global Affairs Correspondent
A news helicopter operated by Angel City Air and providing aerial coverage for NBC Los Angeles and Telemundo 52 crashed Tuesday evening in the Chatsworth neighbourhood of suburban Los Angeles.
The aircraft went down just before 19:00 local time between two commercial buildings, igniting a fierce fire that spread to four vehicles and two storage containers.
More than 70 firefighters rushed to the scene to battle the blaze and assist the victims.
Fatal Toll and Identified Victims
Three people died as a result of the crash, and two others were transported to a local hospital for medical care. The station identified the two crew members on board as aerial photojournalist Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw, whom colleagues remembered as valued friends.
Officials confirmed that a third fatality occurred on the ground when the aircraft came down, though that individual’s identity was withheld pending notification.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass noted the broader human cost of the evening, stating, “We lost five Angelenos today,” referencing both the helicopter disaster and an earlier traffic collision.
Compounding Disasters in Southern California
The helicopter was one of several news aircraft in the area reporting on a severe transit accident that occurred earlier in the day.
A sports utility vehicle collided with a Los Angeles Metro city bus at 17:03 on Nordhoff Street, leaving two people dead and six others injured. First responders were already working near the transit crash site when the aircraft went down shortly before 19:00.
Witnesses near the second scene reported seeing the helicopter behaving erratically before losing altitude and crashing into a massive blaze.
Immediate Reactions and Official Responses
Newsrooms across Southern California reacted with deep shock and grief as confirmation of the disaster emerged during live broadcasts. During emotional live coverage on NBC4, veteran news anchor Colleen Williams told viewers, “We knew it was a news chopper. We knew we’d lost contact with our people out there, and we’ve just received confirmation.”
LAFD Captain Branden Silverman provided early details from the ground, stating, “We do have one confirmed patient that seemed to be outside of the helicopter when it crashed.” Silverman added, “That person was declared deceased on scene.”
Witness Zareh Sevanesian recalled the harrowing moments from the street, noting he told his wife, “That helicopter is not flying right.” He described encountering a chaotic scene near the wreckage, calling it “one of the most violent fires I had ever seen.”
Elected officials extended public condolences via social media and press briefings. The LAPD’s Central Division shared that it extended “thoughts and prayers to the family, friends and colleagues of KNBC 4, Los Angeles.” Mayor Karen Bass expressed that she was “absolutely devastated by the loss of life in Chatsworth tonight,” adding, “My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we lost in the tragic bus collision and helicopter crash.”
California Governor Gavin Newsom also shared a statement, writing that “our hearts are with the victims and families of tonight’s devastating Metro bus and helicopter crashes in Chatsworth, and with the entire NBC4 family,” while offering gratitude to emergency personnel. NBC Los Angeles and Telemundo 52 released a joint statement noting, “We are deeply saddened to share that a helicopter providing aerial news coverage for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 was involved in a fatal accident in Los Angeles on Tuesday evening,” and extended “heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives.”
Ongoing Investigation
Federal aviation authorities have assumed control of the inquiry into why the aircraft went down. The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration will lead the formal investigation to determine the exact sequence of events and cause of the crash.
Broader Context and Industry Impact
Aviation safety experts note that electronic news gathering operations require complex coordination among multiple aircraft in restricted airspace during breaking news events. The dual tragedies in Chatsworth have prompted renewed discussions across Southern California newsrooms regarding the inherent risks faced by aerial journalists and pilots who deliver vital real-time visual context to the public.

sources.news_title: Three killed as NBC news helicopter crashes while covering LA bus accident - OrissaPOST
sources.text:
Los Angeles: A local NBC news helicopter crashed in a Los Angeles neighbourhood on Tuesday and burst into flames, killing at least three people while reporters were covering the nearby crash of an SUV and a city bus, officials and the station said.
Colleen Williams, an NBC4 Los Angeles anchor, confirmed during live broadcasts that the station’s chopper went down just before 7 pm and two people on the helicopter were killed.
“We are going to take a couple of minutes to think about that, process it,” she said, her voice shaking with emotion. Moments later, their coverage abruptly cut off.
Fire officials, Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass and other politicians spoke during a news conference Tuesday night but gave no details on who perished in the crash. After the news conference, the mayor and other officials embraced a crying NBC reporter who also was hugged by fellow journalists.
“Losing five Angelenos is very painful,” Bass said. “And I know this community of Chatsworth was hit hard and will be grieving for some time.”
The helicopter crashed near a large storage facility in the neighbourhood of Chatsworth in the San Fernando Valley, as news crews were covering the bus crash that left at least two people dead and six others injured, according to the Los Angeles Fire Department.
At least one person killed in the helicopter crash was outside in the parking lot next to the commercial building, said Capt. Branden Silverman, a spokesperson for the Los Angeles Fire Department.
Two people were transported to a hospital, said Rico A. Gross, a fire department battalion chief. Their conditions were not immediately released.
“From the helicopter itself, it’s pretty well destroyed,” Silverman said. “So we are going to have to go through the rubble and see how many victims there were on board, as well as identify the helicopter; we couldn’t even see a tail.”
At least four cars and two storage containers on the ground burned after the helicopter caught fire, which was quickly put out, according to officials. More than 70 firefighters responded to the helicopter crash, according to the fire department. Dozens of police cars surrounded the scene at the storage facility as ambulances entered.
About two hours before the crash, an SUV slammed into the middle of a city bus, killing at least two people and injuring six others. Photos and videos online showed half the SUV lodged into the side of an MTA bus.
NBC has confirmed the helicopter was NewsChopper4, which is operated by Angel City Air, and was used by NBCLA and Telemundo 52. The outlet said several TV news helicopters were reporting on the bus crash before the news chopper went down about 2.4 kilometres from the bus collision.
NBC4 and Telemundo 52 Los Angeles said in a statement they “are deeply saddened” to learn of the helicopter crash and extended “heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives.”
Gov. Gavin Newsom thanked the emergency crews responding to both crashes and said in a post on X that “our hearts are with the victims and families.”
The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration said they will be investigating the cause of the helicopter crash and would be sending one of its investigators on Wednesday.
There have been at least eight fatal crashes involving news helicopters in the US since 2000, killing 16 people, according to a review of federal accident records and news accounts.
They include a 2023 crash in a New Jersey forest that killed the pilot and a photographer aboard a helicopter used by Philadelphia station WPVI and a 2022 crash beside a Charlotte, North Carolina, interstate that killed a pilot and meteorologist during a training flight for WBTV.
